units.translation: A word undoubtedly formed by Aeschylus, if he wrote it thus, for πρόβουλος παῖς [a child who is a counselor], like εὐφιλόπαις [dear to children] below at 723. "These words have been badly understood by many. He says, 'Persuasion, the audacious counselor, the unbridled daughter of Ruin, urges one to rush into destruction. For once guilt has been admitted, it persuades one to bring to bear the work and power to protect what is unjustly possessed, and supplies plans for that purpose.' These words refer to what immediately precedes, and Persuasion is called πρόβουλος [a counselor] because she seeks an ἔπαλξιν πλούτου [a bulwark of wealth]." HERMANN. Similarly Klausen interprets: "the guilt that has injured the mind begets persuasion that supplies arguments by which one is moved to carry out the plans of guilt." The scholion of Thomas Magister is: ἥτις (ἡ Πειθώ) βιάζει αὐτοὺς πρόνοιαν δῆθεν τοῦ πλουτῆσαι (πλουτίσαι Victorius) τοὺς παῖδας ποιουμένη [who (Persuasion) forces them, pretending to have forethought for enriching (to enrich Victorius) the children], and that of Triclinius: ἡ προβουλευομένη πλουτῆσαι τοὺς παῖδας [she who plans beforehand to enrich the children]. Karsten and Weil wrongly wrote βιᾶται δ᾽ ἁ τάλαινα πειθὼ πρόβουλος, παῖς ἄφερτος ἄτας [and wretched Persuasion, the counselor, the unbridled child of Ruin, forces], (and in the strophic verse 368 πάρεστιν for πάρεστι), which is a faulty punctuation, into which no one can fall unless warned by a comma placed after πρόβουλος. Hartung is better: πειθώ, προβούλου παῖς ἄφερτος ἄτας [Persuasion, unbridled child of Ruin the counselor]. For Ruin gives the plans, to the execution of which Persuasion compels. Rightly, therefore, Persuasion is said to be the daughter of Ruin the counselor. Similarly Todt in his Commentary p. 34.
And wretched Persuasion forces, the counselor-child, unbridled, of Ruin.
